scenes.visual: Title card 'Wings Faster Than Nerves' over a blurred-wing fly silhouette. Reuses the first film's COLOUR MAP: actin BLUE, myosin ORANGE, calcium YELLOW dots, tropomyosin DARK GREY, ATP GREEN, store PALE TEAL. New for this film: nerve impulse spikes RED on the trace, wingbeat ticks GREY, thorax a CREAM springy box, the two power-muscle sets drawn as ORANGE-striped bands labelled 'set A' and 'set B'. Everything here is a cartoon; traces are labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: Does every wingbeat need its own nerve impulse? A fly beats its wings so fast that the answer seemed in doubt. One recording put it to the test.
scenes.visual: A fly hovers, wings a blur. A small nerve drawn as a cable runs into its thorax, flashing RED once per wingbeat, then stuttering as the wings speed up. Question card: 'One impulse per beat?'
scenes.narration: Does every wingbeat need its own nerve impulse? A fly beats its wings so fast that the answer seemed in doubt. One recording put it to the test.

scenes.tts: The first film built one machine. Calcium switches it on, and myosin heads pull actin. Now the question is how a fly's flight muscle throws that switch.
scenes.visual: Brief replay of the first film's sarcomere: YELLOW dots arrive, DARK GREY strand rolls aside, ORANGE heads pull BLUE filaments inward. A YELLOW switch icon zooms out of it and sits beside the fly.
scenes.narration: The first film built one machine. Calcium switches it on, and myosin heads pull actin. Now the question is how a fly's flight muscle throws that switch.

scenes.tts: In vertebrate skeletal muscle, each contraction follows its own nerve impulse. So does the flight muscle of a locust or a dragonfly. This is called synchronous muscle.
scenes.visual: A locust cartoon flaps slowly. Under it a trace scrolls: one RED spike lines up exactly under each GREY wingbeat tick, joined by thin vertical lines. Label 'synchronous: one impulse, one contraction'.
scenes.narration: In vertebrate skeletal muscle, each contraction follows its own nerve impulse. So does the flight muscle of a locust or a dragonfly. This is called synchronous muscle.

scenes.tts: In nineteen forty-nine, John Pringle tested this rule in blue-bottle flies. He tethered each fly so that it beat its wings in place. Then he put a fine electrode into its flight muscle.
scenes.visual: Caption 'J. W. S. Pringle, 1949'. A blue-bottle fly is held by a rod glued to its back, wings beating. A fine needle enters its thorax and a wire runs to a plain recording box. A blank trace window opens with a row of GREY wingbeat ticks along its top.
scenes.narration: In nineteen forty-nine, John Pringle tested this rule in blue-bottle flies. He tethered each fly so that it beat its wings in place. Then he put a fine electrode into its flight muscle.

scenes.tts: If every beat needs its own impulse, the trace should show one large spike under every wingbeat. What do you think he saw?
scenes.visual: Twenty GREY ticks across the trace window. Faint dashed RED outlines sit under every tick, labelled 'predicted: one large spike per beat'. Question card.
scenes.narration: If every beat needs its own impulse, the trace should show one large spike under every wingbeat. What do you think he saw?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. Question card holds; 5-second ring timer at bottom right.

scenes.tts: The large spikes, which he linked to nerve impulses, came far less often than the wings beat. And they were not timed to particular beats. The one-to-one rule failed.
scenes.visual: The trace draws itself: small blips under every GREY tick, but only a few tall RED spikes, scattered at irregular places, not lined up with ticks. The dashed outlines fade. Label 'schematic trace: far fewer large spikes than wingbeats'.
scenes.narration: The large spikes, which he linked to nerve impulses, came far less often than the wings beat. And they were not timed to particular beats. The one-to-one rule failed.

scenes.tts: So what sets the beat? Picture the fly's thorax as a springy box. Two sets of power muscles pull on it in different directions.
scenes.visual: Cutaway of the thorax as a CREAM box with springy walls. Band 'set A' runs front to back; band 'set B' runs top to bottom. The wings stick out at the sides as hinged paddles.
scenes.narration: So what sets the beat? Picture the fly's thorax as a springy box. Two sets of power muscles pull on it in different directions.

scenes.tts: When one set shortens, the box bends, and the other set is stretched. These muscles are already switched on. In them, a stretch raises force, after a short delay.
scenes.visual: Set A shortens; the box deforms and set B visibly lengthens, label 'stretched'. Both sets keep a faint steady YELLOW glow, label 'already switched on'. A small clock icon ticks on set B before its stripes brighten, label 'stretch, then delay, then more force'.
scenes.narration: When one set shortens, the box bends, and the other set is stretched. These muscles are already switched on. In them, a stretch raises force, after a short delay.

scenes.tts: So the stretched set builds force and shortens. That stretches the first set in turn. The muscles and the springy thorax keep the rhythm going between them.
scenes.visual: Set B shortens; the box bends the other way and set A is stretched, its clock ticks, it brightens and shortens. The two sets alternate several times; the wings flap with each swing. A looping arrow labelled 'muscle + thorax set the beat'.
scenes.narration: So the stretched set builds force and shortens. That stretches the first set in turn. The muscles and the springy thorax keep the rhythm going between them.

scenes.tts: This is asynchronous muscle. It powers the wings of flies, bees and wasps, beetles and some other insects. In nineteen fifty-nine, Machin and Pringle reported stretch activation in beetle flight muscle.
scenes.visual: Label 'asynchronous muscle'. Small cartoons of a fly, a bee, a wasp and a beetle appear in a row. Caption 'Machin and Pringle, 1959: isolated beetle flight muscle is activated by stretch'.
scenes.narration: This is asynchronous muscle. It powers the wings of flies, bees and wasps, beetles and some other insects. In nineteen fifty-nine, Machin and Pringle reported stretch activation in beetle flight muscle.

scenes.tts: Does that make the nerve useless? No. Its few impulses keep the muscle's calcium raised, so it stays switched on. Without them, the wings stop.
scenes.visual: Back in the thorax: occasional RED impulses arrive along the nerve cable, and the YELLOW dots inside both muscle sets stay high throughout, label 'calcium kept up'. Then the nerve is cut with scissors: the YELLOW dots drain away, the sets go still, the wings stop.
scenes.narration: Does that make the nerve useless? No. Its few impulses keep the muscle's calcium raised, so it stays switched on. Without them, the wings stop.

scenes.tts: The pulling machine is the same as in the first film. What changed is the switch. The nerve holds it on, and stretch times each beat.
scenes.visual: Split screen: left, the first film's sarcomere with a YELLOW switch flicked once per RED impulse, label 'synchronous'. Right, the same sarcomere with the YELLOW switch held on and a spring icon adding extra force to each pull, label 'asynchronous'.
scenes.narration: The pulling machine is the same as in the first film. What changed is the switch. The nerve holds it on, and stretch times each beat.

scenes.tts: Pringle's recordings left questions open. And how stretch raises force, at the level of the molecules, is still being worked out.
scenes.visual: A notebook page with two open questions written in: 'Were the large spikes full action potentials?' and 'How does stretch raise force?' A small 'still being worked out' stamp on the second.
scenes.narration: Pringle's recordings left questions open. And how stretch raises force, at the level of the molecules, is still being worked out.

scenes.tts: So here is the rule for these insects. In asynchronous muscle, stretch times each beat, and the nerve keeps it on.
scenes.visual: The springy box with sets A and B alternating, a steady YELLOW glow inside, and sparse RED impulses on the nerve. The rule line types out beneath.
scenes.narration: So here is the rule for these insects. In asynchronous muscle, stretch times each beat, and the nerve keeps it on.

scenes.visual: End card with the mascot and one line only: 'In asynchronous muscle, stretch times each beat; the nerve keeps it on.'
